opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that most benchmarks are built around a fairly narrow band of task difficulty. When you design a benchmark, you typically pick a collection of problems that are hard for current systems but not completely out of reach, because otherwise you can't distinguish between models at all. The problem is that AI capabilities have been improving so quickly that this band gets crossed very fast. So what you tend to see is a benchmark sitting near zero for a while, then there's a relatively brief period where scores shoot up, and then it saturates near the ceiling. If you plot that over time you get something like a sigmoid rather than a smooth line, and the informative part of the curve might only span a year or two.

Part of the reason for that is the distribution of difficulty within a benchmark is usually quite compressed. If all the questions are roughly similar in how hard they are, then once a model gets good enough to solve one type, it can solve most of them. To get smooth progress you'd want problems spanning many orders of magnitude of difficulty, so that at any given level of capability there's always a frontier of problems that are just barely being solved. But constructing that is really hard, because it's not obvious how to measure difficulty in a way that's stable across very different kinds of systems. Something that's hard for humans isn't necessarily hard for a language model, and vice versa.

There's also the issue that a lot of progress comes from qualitative shifts. A model might suddenly become able to do multi-step reasoning, or use tools, or check its own work, and that unlocks a whole class of problems at once. Benchmarks that implicitly test for one of those capabilities will show a jump rather than a gradual climb.

And then there are practical problems: contamination, where benchmark data ends up in training sets; labs optimizing specifically for well-known benchmarks; and noise in the questions themselves, where some fraction are ambiguous or mislabeled, which puts an artificial ceiling below 100%. All of these distort the curve.

So if you want something that tracks progress smoothly over long periods, you probably need to think more carefully about measures that are inherently open-ended, like the length or complexity of tasks a system can complete autonomously, or economic value generated, rather than a fixed set of questions. Those have their own measurement problems, but at least they don't have a built-in ceiling that you'll hit in eighteen months.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons, and they're kind of layered on top of each other.

The first one is just the basic structure of a benchmark. You pick a set of tasks, you fix them, and then you measure what fraction of them a model can do. The problem is that a fixed set of tasks only has a certain range of difficulty baked into it. When models are far below that range, you get scores near zero or near random chance, and you can't distinguish between models because they're all failing. Then there's a fairly narrow window where the models are in the right difficulty band and you actually see movement. And then once they're past it, you saturate at the ceiling and again you can't distinguish anything. So almost by construction, any benchmark gives you this S-shaped curve where most of the informative signal is concentrated in a short period of time, maybe a year or two, and outside that window it's flat. That looks like discontinuous progress even if the underlying capabilities are improving fairly smoothly.

The second reason is that people who design benchmarks are usually trying to make them hard for current models. That's the natural thing to do, because if your benchmark is already saturated it's not interesting. But that means you're deliberately picking tasks right at the frontier, in the zone where models are mostly failing. And then when models cross that threshold, they tend to cross it quickly, because the tasks were selected to be roughly uniform in difficulty relative to current capabilities rather than spread across a wide range. If you wanted smooth progress, you'd want tasks spanning many orders of magnitude of difficulty, but that's hard to do in practice because the easy tasks are boring and the very hard tasks are hard to even write and verify.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that difficulty isn't one-dimensional. A benchmark is usually measuring some particular skill, or some bundle of skills, and progress on the underlying model doesn't improve all skills at the same rate. So you might have a benchmark that's bottlenecked on, say, long-context reasoning, or on a specific kind of knowledge, or on the model being able to use tools reliably. And then nothing happens for a while, and then some change in training unblocks that specific bottleneck and the benchmark jumps. From the perspective of the benchmark that looks like a discontinuity, but from the perspective of the overall system it's just one component catching up.

And then there's the measurement side. Benchmarks are noisy, they get contaminated, people change the evaluation harness, they add scaffolding, they use more inference compute. All of that adds jumps that have nothing to do with the smooth trend you care about.

So what you'd actually want, if your goal is to see smooth progress, is something that isn't a fixed task set at all. Something more like measuring the length or complexity of tasks that models can do with some fixed success rate, where the scale is open-ended and you can keep extending it as models improve. Some people have started doing things like that, and you do get something closer to a smooth exponential. But it's much more work than writing a few hundred questions and checking answers, and it comes with its own problems around how you define task difficulty in a way that's comparable over time. So my view is that smooth-looking progress isn't absent, it's just that the standard benchmark format is almost designed to hide it.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that a benchmark usually measures a fairly narrow range of difficulty. When models are below that range, they all do badly, so you don’t see much progress. Then they become good enough to solve the tasks, scores rise quite quickly, and eventually the benchmark saturates. You stop seeing progress again, even if the underlying capabilities are continuing to improve.

For example, imagine testing people’s mathematical ability using only problems from a single school year. That test might distinguish students at that level quite well, but it won’t tell you much about differences between beginners or between professional mathematicians. To measure progress over a long period, you need questions spanning a very wide range of difficulty.

With AI, the additional challenge is that we don’t know in advance what that range should look like. A task that seems extremely difficult today might become easy with the next generation of models, while another task that looks simple might remain difficult. So it’s hard to construct a fixed benchmark that will remain informative—and show smooth progress—across many generations of systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main problem is that progress is smooth in some underlying capabilities, but the relationship between those capabilities and performance on a particular task can be quite nonlinear. If a task requires several things to go right, a model might improve at all of them and still fail the task almost every time. Then, once it gets good enough, its success rate can rise very quickly. So you see something that looks like a sudden jump, even though the underlying improvements were gradual.

You can try to address that by having a benchmark with lots of questions at different difficulty levels. But then you need those difficulties to be distributed appropriately over the range of models you’re going to evaluate. That’s hard to anticipate. You might end up with a lot of questions that are too easy and a lot that are too hard, with very little in between.

And once models start doing well on a benchmark, it stops telling you very much about further progress. So you’re constantly having to introduce harder evaluations, and then there’s a question of how you compare those to the old ones. It’s much easier to measure progress over a limited range than to construct one benchmark that stays informative over a long period of time.
